Nadudvar Jewish Cemetery 1

Jewish Cemetery · Nádudvar, Hungary

Not demolished. One of two Jewish cemeteries in Nádudvar, one of the oldest Jewish communities in the region. Sources disagree on this cemetery's exact founding: one dates it to 1750, when the first Jews arrived; another claims early-1700s origins, when it also served neighboring Kaba and Földes communities lacking their own cemeteries. Tax census records confirm Jews present by 1770, matching the oldest tombstones' dating. Population reached 84 by 1786; in 1794, the famous Rabbi Eisig Taub of Nagykálló personally petitioned to rebuild the collapsed local synagogue, restored by public donation in 1802. The organized community, formed in 1806, employed a butcher and teacher; by 1852, 412 of the town's 6,877 residents were Jewish. Rabbi Mayer Rosenfeld's 1860 installation prompted construction of a mikveh; a Jewish public school opened in 1873, closing in 1925 when state subsidies ended. Population peaked at 505 by 1900; a 1920 plaque honored fallen WWI soldiers. In 1941, 210 Jews remained; in 1944, all local Jews (joined by Kaba's community) were forced into the synagogue-turned-ghetto before deportation to Debrecen, with a small group sent to Austria. Survivors returned to erect a memorial, briefly rebuilding a 56-person community before near-total departure left no Jews in Nádudvar by 1953. Between 2012-2015, the Heritage Foundation for Preservation of Jewish Cemeteries restored the site, clearing it and rebuilding two small ohel buildings.
